text: Many animals have evolved. <break time="0.8s" /> Mechanisms for picking out signals from the noise. <break time="0.8s" /> Imagine being in a crowded restaurant. <break time="0.8s" /> With everyone clustered in the middle of the room. <break time="0.8s" /> Talking in loud voices at once. <break time="0.8s" /> No one can hear anything. <break time="0.8s" /> Now imagine, instead. <break time="0.8s" /> People organizing themselves into groups by language. <break time="0.8s" /> English, Cree, French, Hindi, Spanish, Swahili. <break time="0.8s" /> And moving to different parts of the room. <break time="0.8s" /> Standing in the center of the room. <break time="0.8s" /> Your mind will tune into the group that speaks languages that you personally understand. <break time="0.8s" /> And filter out the rest. <break time="0.8s" /> In finding a niche. <break time="0.8s" /> Each group gains relative tranquility. <break time="0.8s" /> Rather than cacophony. <break time="0.8s" /> Tuning into recognizable sounds. <break time="0.8s" /> And tuning out unintelligible ones. <break time="0.8s" /> The listener expends less energy. <break time="0.8s" /> In nature. <break time="0.8s" /> Species adopt a similar tactic. <break time="0.8s" /> As species evolve their ability to hear. <break time="0.8s" /> They also evolve. <break time="0.8s" /> To favor specific frequencies. <break time="0.8s" /> If one species sings in high tones. <break time="0.8s" /> And another sings in low tones. <break time="0.8s" /> It is easier. <break time="0.8s" /> For members of each species. <break time="0.8s" /> To pick out the signal from the noise. <break time="0.8s" /> In any ecosystem. <break time="0.8s" /> Different species partition themselves. <break time="0.8s" /> In time, acoustic frequency, or space. <break time="0.8s" /> To reduce competition for different parts of the soundscape spectrum.
